items.title: The Evolution of Big Data Architectures: From Traditional Data Management to Data Lakehouses
items.abstract: The rapid growth in data volume, variety, and generation speed has led to a significant transformation in data management architectures. This study examines the evolution of Big Data architectures from traditional file-based systems and relational databases to Data Warehouses, Data Lakes, and Data Lakehouses. The main characteristics, data processing approaches, advantages, and limitations of these architectures are discussed comparatively. The study also examines cloud-based Big Data platforms, distributed data processing technologies such as Apache Spark and Apache Kafka, and the integration of Big Data with Business Intelligence and Artificial Intelligence applications. In addition, current challenges such as data quality, metadata management, data governance, and the risk of Data Lakes becoming Data Swamps are discussed. Finally, the study highlights the management of data structures required by Machine Learning applications and high-dimensional data as important research topics for the future development of Data Lake and Lakehouse architectures.

items.title: The evolution of radiographers—an investigation into radiographers’ role and perspectives: a EuroAIM/EFRS survey
items.abstract: Abstract Radiographers play a central role within clinical imaging and radiotherapy teams, acting as a key interface between patients and increasingly complex technologies. As healthcare systems evolve, their scope of practice is expanding alongside advances in digital workflows, artificial intelligence (AI) and new models of care. This EuroAIM/EFRS survey provides a comprehensive European overview of radiographers’ roles, professional autonomy, research engagement and perspectives on AI. Based on responses from 1548 radiographers across multiple countries, the findings highlight substantial clinical autonomy and strong responsibility for image quality optimisation and radiation protection, alongside limited but growing involvement in research activities. More than half of the participants expressed interest in greater research participation, indicating a gap between current opportunities and professional aspirations. Responses regarding AI were generally positive, with many participants expecting it to enhance their professional roles, although expectations regarding its workforce impact remained heterogeneous. The survey also confirms the lasting effects of the COVID-19 pandemic on professional practice and highlights variability in perceived career development opportunities. These findings describe a profession in transition, characterised by increasing responsibilities and technological integration and underscore the need for continued investment in education, structured career frameworks and research capacity to support radiographers in an increasingly complex healthcare environment. Key Points Question What are radiographers’ current roles, autonomy, research engagement and perspectives on emerging technologies within a changing imaging and radiotherapy workforce? Findings In 1548 participants, radiographers reported substantial autonomy and responsibility, limited research involvement, positive but heterogeneous AI expectations and variable career opportunities. Critical Relevance Statement This EuroAIM/EFRS survey informs radiology practice by identifying radiographers’ professional development, education and research needs and by supporting structured career frameworks and interprofessional workforce planning.

items.title: The Future of Work for Women Workers on Digital Labour Platforms in India: A Doctrinal Analysis of the Labour Codes in Light of ILO Convention No. 193, with Bangladesh as Comparator
items.abstract: Digital labour platforms are often celebrated for offering flexible work, yet women platform workers remain marginal in both regulation and legal scholarship. This article asks a single doctrinal question: when the law recognises platform workers without treating them as employees, which gender-relevant labour entitlements actually reach women? India is the primary jurisdiction. We examine the Code on Social Security, 2020, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Code on Wages, 2019 and the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act, 2013, as operationalised by the Social Security (Central) Rules, 2026. Bangladesh, which reformed its Labour Act, 2006 through the 2025 Ordinance and the Bangladesh Labour (Amendment) Act, 2026, serves as a comparator that entered platform regulation by the opposite route. Both are measured against the ILO Decent Work in the Platform Economy Convention, 2026 (No. 193), read with the Violence and Harassment Convention, 2019 (No. 190) and the Maternity Protection Convention, 2000 (No. 183). Using a doctrinal comparative method with a stated source-selection protocol, and a three-step test for regulatory gender blindness, we analyse four criteria: personal scope, maternity protection, protection against violence and harassment, and equality in algorithmic management and collective voice. We find that India recognises platform workers through welfare schemes without status, while Bangladesh recognises them through collective rights without social insurance; in neither jurisdiction does statutory maternity benefit reach a woman platform worker, because it remains tied to the employer and the establishment. Facially neutral qualifying conditions, notably India’s 90/120-day engagement rule, operate to the particular disadvantage of women, and of women in home-based care and beauty work most of all. Convention No. 193 narrows but does not close these gaps, since its social security guarantee is one of parity within the same employment classification. We conclude with prioritised, instrument-specific reforms.

items.title: The Happy vs. The Afraid
items.abstract: The Happy vs. The Afraid investigates the distinction between apparent fulfillment through personally meaningful activity and behavior motivated by expectations, responsibilities, or perceived consequences. The paper introduces an observer-relative conceptual framework examining two motivational orientations: engagement driven by curiosity, enjoyment, and personal meaning, and engagement influenced by obligation, external expectations, or the avoidance of undesirable outcomes. Section One presents a biographical examination of professional falconer and conservation advocate Nathalie Denolf, exploring her documented career, relationship with birds of prey, public educational work, and expressed dedication to animal welfare. An accompanying author's note examines the evolutionary continuity between non-avian dinosaurs and modern birds. Section Two develops the conceptual distinction between the Happy and the Afraid through the author's symbolic framework: i — Intuitive: Curiosity, personal meaning, and spontaneous engagement. I — Independent: Autonomy, self-direction, and individual choice. O — Obligation: Responsibility, expectation, and perceived consequence. Section Three introduces a comparative observational study of three public educators whom the author perceives as demonstrating visible enthusiasm for subjects of personal interest. The two additional case studies remain pending identification and completion in this working version. Drawing upon established research in intrinsic motivation, self-determination theory, and approach-avoidance motivation, the paper examines how observers distinguish apparent passion from obligation while acknowledging the limitations of interpreting another person's internal emotional experience. The central proposition is not that individuals can be objectively categorized as happy or afraid, but that the observer's own experiences, interests, and expectations influence how human engagement is understood.

items.title: The Healthy Organisation for the 1990s
items.abstract: This chapter examines the meaning of a ‘healthy organization’ in conditions of turbulence and uncertainty characteristic of the 1990s. Drawing on Tavistock socio-technical and psychoanalytic traditions, Eric Miller distinguishes between health as an individual attribute and organizational health as a systemic property arising from the interaction of task, sentient, and boundary systems. Organizations are viewed as operating within internal and external environments marked by instability and change, requiring structures that provide sufficient psychological security for effective role performance. Revisiting the evolution of occupational health, the chapter argues that organizational design must address psychosocial as well as technical factors. Miller extends socio-technical systems theory by differentiating task systems that deliver work, sentient systems that meet needs for identity and affiliation, and boundary systems that regulate their relationship. Central to organizational health is the creation of an appropriate ‘holding environment,’ enabling members to manage anxiety while remaining engaged with demanding tasks. Case examples from people-processing organizations illustrate how inadequate holding environments undermine morale and effectiveness, and how restoring supervision, support, and participation can rapidly improve organizational functioning. The chapter highlights the paradox of fostering psychological security in contexts of job insecurity and rapid change. A healthy organization is thus defined not by stability or comfort, but by its capacity to contain anxiety, support learning, and sustain effective performance amid ongoing turbulence.

items.title: The Hidden Curriculum of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Abstract This chapter investigates the potential impact of biases present in large language models (LLMs) on students’ creative experiences. Using a case study design with fictional student scenarios and simulated prompts, the chapter analyzes LLM responses for variations based on student-expressed music preferences (rap or classical), which can serve as implicit indicators of race and socioeconomic status. Both Linguistic Inquiry Word Count (LIWC) analysis and manual coding were employed to examine the language used by LLMs, focusing on exploratory versus directive statements. Results indicate that LLMs tend to use more direct and authoritative language and exhibit less positive tone when responding to prompts associated with rap music, potentially reinforcing societal inequities and the hidden curriculum of schooling. This suggests that biases in LLMs could differentially impact students’ creative experiences and development, highlighting the need for critical awareness and mitigation strategies in educational AI applications. The chapter discusses the international implications of these findings, considering how Western-centric training data may shape LLM responses in ways that marginalize underrepresented users globally.

items.title: The Hidden Trade-Offs
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is revolutionizing human functioning with profound consequences for creativity and education. Because creativity is an activity that stems from agency—confidence in one’s ability to solve problems, the centrality of being creative to a person’s identity, the willingness to explore risky paths, and the ability to self-regulate—this chapter overviews the chances and challenges that using GenAI might pose for people’s creative agency. Moreover, based on research indicating that GenAI models can score people’s responses in various creativity tasks in real time, the chapter discusses the opportunities of using AI as a feedback provider that might allow people to learn and improve. Although such formative assessment and training are promising in stimulating people’s creativity, they do not come without costs. The chapter also provides a series of practical recommendations for using AI to make it an efficient creativity-enhancing tool.

items.title: The Human Element
items.abstract: In The Human Element , Eric J. Miller examines the profound organizational and psychological consequences of introducing new technology into work systems. Drawing on Tavistock Institute research and cross-industry experience, Miller challenges the assumption of technological determinism, arguing that technology does not dictate a single form of organization. Instead, managers face choices in how work is structured, many of which have decisive implications for productivity, morale, and commitment. Central to the chapter is the concept of the socio-technical system, in which effective performance depends on the interaction between social and technical systems. Miller emphasizes the principle of joint optimization: improving technology alone, or focusing solely on human relations, leads to suboptimal outcomes. Successful change requires designing work systems that accommodate human skills, values, and group dynamics as integral components of production. The chapter explores the effects of technological change on individuals, workgroups, and organizations. It highlights the risks of disrupting established social systems, the limitations of purely ergonomic job design, and the vulnerability of highly automated systems to human stress and error. Miller advocates self-regulating work groups as a means of enhancing control, learning, and responsibility. In conclusion, Miller argues that new technologies demand a rethinking of managerial roles, authority, and organizational design. Managing technological change is fundamentally a social task, requiring leadership willing to confront uncertainty, redesign systems, and engage people as active contributors rather than passive operators.

items.title: The Impact of AI-Powered Coding Tools on Students' Learning Habits and Programming
items.abstract: AI coding assistants can generate code, explain programming concepts, and suggest debugging steps, but their educational value cannot be judged from task completion alone. This focused narrative review examines how AI-assisted programming relates to students’ learning behavior, programming performance, independent problem-solving, and psychological processes. It synthesizes recent empirical studies and reviews, including a meta-analysis of 35 controlled studies, a systematic review of 119 papers on AI in programming education, a quasiexperiment with 82 college students, a study of 17 novice programmers, and a randomized controlled trial with 275 students. Across this evidence, AI assistance is often associated with improved performance or efficiency on supported tasks, but gains in conceptual understanding and independent learning are less consistent. Behavioral Science helps explain this distinction through cognitive load, programming self-efficacy, frustration, intrinsic motivation, help-seeking, and metacognitive monitoring. A recent trial found that AI-supported groups performed better on a programming exercise than a no-AI group, yet did not show greater short-term knowledge gains or code-comprehension scores. The review argues that the instructional design of AI support matters: hint-first scaffolding, code verification, explanation, retrieval practice, and independent transfer tasks are more defensible than unrestricted answer generation as default teaching strategies. Because this paper is a focused narrative review, it does not claim exhaustive systematic coverage or report original student data.

items.title: The Impact of AI-Supported Smart Learning Environments on Interaction, Achievement, and Self-Learning Skills among Higher Education Students in Kuwait: A Field Study
items.abstract: This study examined the impact of AI-supported smart learning environments on academic interaction, achievement, and self-learning skills among higher education students in Kuwait. A descriptive analytical approach was employed, and data were collected from higher education students using a questionnaire measuring their perceptions of AI-supported smart learning environments and their effects on learning outcomes. The findings revealed that AI-supported smart learning environments had a significant positive impact on students’ academic interaction, achievement, and self-learning skills. The results also indicated that integrating artificial intelligence into learning environments enhanced students’ engagement with learning activities, supported independent learning, and contributed to improved academic performance. Furthermore, AI-supported smart learning environments provided flexible and interactive learning experiences that addressed students’ individual learning needs. These findings highlight the potential of artificial intelligence to enhance the quality of higher education and support more student-centered learning. The study recommends expanding the integration of AI technologies into higher education institutions while providing appropriate training and technical support for faculty members and students. items.title: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence on Organizational Change Processes: A New Change Management Paradigm?
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer merely used as a new technological tool in organizations; it is becoming one of the constitutive elements of decision-making, coordination, control, knowledge production, work design, and employee experience. This development raises the question of whether AI, beyond being an object of organizational change, is transforming how change emerges, by whom it is directed, and over what time horizon it is managed. The aim of this chapter is to critically evaluate the explanatory power of established change management approaches in the age of AI and to develop an integrated conceptual framework for explaining AI-mediated organizational change. Lewin’s planned change approach, Kotter’s model, organizational development, continuous change, organizational learning, dynamic capabilities, socio-technical systems, and technology acceptance approaches are compared in the context of AI’s learnability, partial autonomy, opacity, and scalability. The conceptual synthesis indicates that the mechanisms of leadership, participation, communication, trust, and institutionalization emphasized by established approaches remain valid; however, assumptions of linear processes, a clearly defined end state, exclusively human agency, and one-off implementation are inadequate. The “double-loop AI change governance” model proposed in this chapter integrates the redesign of organizational task and decision architectures with monitoring the AI system throughout its life cycle in terms of performance, errors, fairness, and employee impacts. In conclusion, it is argued that it is premature to declare that AI constitutes an entirely new paradigm; nevertheless, it necessitates a substantial paradigm extension that reconceptualizes change management as a continuous, distributed, data-informed, and socio-technical governance capability.

items.title: THE IMPACT OF DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES ON THE DEVELOPMENT OF TRANSPORT INFRASTRUCTURE
items.abstract: Purpose. The article investigates the impact of digital technologies on the transport infrastructure of modern cities. It substantiates strategic directions and priorities for implementing intelligent transport systems (ITS) amid intensifying urbanization and growing pressure on transport networks. Methodology. The study applies systems analysis, treating transport infrastructure as an integral sociotechnical system. It is complemented by a comparative analysis of documented ITS deployments in the United States (Los Angeles), Singapore, the Republic of Korea (Seoul), and the Netherlands (Amsterdam), which represent decentralized, centralized-state, and supranationally coordinated (European Union) governance contexts; by a structural-functional analysis of ITS architecture; and by induction and deduction for formulating generalizations. Findings. Published evaluations associate ITS deployments with reductions in travel time of about 12–13%, in intersection delay of 21–32%, in vehicle stops of about 30% and in air emissions of about 10% (Los Angeles), with higher traffic speeds under dynamic road pricing (Singapore), with fewer bus-related accidents (Seoul) and with fewer vehicle loss hours (Amsterdam). The cases point to three institutional preconditions: a coordinating strategic framework, partnership between public authorities and the private sector, and open standards for inter-system data exchange. Originality. The article proposes a conceptual model that integrates the architectural, institutional, and financial dimensions of transport digitalization, along with a four-stage model for implementing ITS adapted to the conditions of transitional economies. Practical value. items.title: The impact of the data factor platform on the urban green innovation: evidence from China
items.abstract: Abstract With the rapid expansion of the digital economy, data elements have emerged as a pivotal force shaping urban green development. This study offers a novel perspective by examining how the construction of data factor platform influences urban green innovation. From the channel of artificial intelligence (AI) development and human capital accumulation, we propose a mechanism framework. Based on the city-level data from 2010 to 2022 in China, using the multi-period Difference-in-Difference (DID) model, we explore the impact of the data factor platform construction on urban green innovation. The results reveal that data factor platform construction can stimulate urban green innovation. The data factor platform construction stimulates urban green innovation through the channel of promoting AI development and accelerating human capital accumulation. The impact of the data factor platform construction on the urban green innovation is heterogeneous. The data factor platform construction has a larger effect on the urban green innovation in the low-carbon pilot city situation and cities with larger economic scales. The further analysis results reveal that the data factor platform construction in the surrounding areas effectively promotes local green innovation. According to the above conclusions, in the green transition process, the government should pay attention to data factor platform programs and make a combination of policies to stimulate green innovations.

items.title: The important role of furniture in our lives.
items.abstract: Furniture is far more than a collection of functional objects; it serves as an essential bridge between human needs, cultural identity, psychological well-being, and environmental sustainability. This article examines the multifaceted role of furniture in daily life, from its historical evolution to its contemporary impact on health, productivity, social interactions, and interior spaces. Drawing on global design principles and Uzbek scholarly perspectives, it highlights how furniture shapes lifestyles, influences emotions, and addresses modern challenges such as urbanization and ergonomic demands. Through a comprehensive literature review and analytical discussion, the study underscores furniture’s transformative power in enhancing comfort, promoting health, and reflecting societal values. The findings emphasize the need for innovative, culturally sensitive, and sustainable design practices to meet future demands. This work contributes to a deeper understanding of furniture as a vital element of human existence, offering insights for designers, architects, and consumers alike.

items.title: The intelligence loop and value creation in the age of AI agents
items.abstract: Abstract Research Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving from generating outputs to executing work. An agent that executes work autonomously produces something generative AI does not: operational experience that can raise its future intelligence. Prior research on AI emphasizes value creation through demand‐side feedback, notably data network effects, in which user data improve prediction and reinforce adoption. We develop the supply‐side counterpart, the intelligence loop: delegated usage generates operational experience, agentic capability converts it into future intelligence, and the resulting value maintains or expands usage. The loop cannot operate until autonomous execution is viable, a threshold we call minimum viable intelligence (MVI). Crossing MVI does not guarantee rising intelligence. Comparable deployments of AI agents can diverge as their loops decay, sustain, or accelerate. Three implications follow. Competitive advantage may depend more on the loop than on installed base. An above‐MVI agent supplies scarce expert skill as a non‐rival, replicable resource, so productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount, with the one‐person company as a limiting case. And a venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can still fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Managerial Summary Artificial intelligence (AI) agents can execute work, and the experience generated through execution can raise their future intelligence, a feedback process we call the intelligence loop. An agent crosses a workflow's minimum viable intelligence (MVI) when it executes reliably without step‐by‐step direction, autonomous execution creates at least as much net value as the best alternative after oversight and correction costs, and governance arrangements keep residual risk acceptable and accountability clear. Investment belongs where one of these conditions keeps a valuable workflow below MVI. Deployment can begin with narrow, feedback‐rich workflows near MVI that ideally lead to harder workflows, since base model upgrades can match gains on simple work. Even above MVI, the loop is not automatic: it stalls when feedback is not timely and diagnostic, experience yields little intelligence gain, gains add little user value, or value does not maintain or expand usage. Human involvement shifts from executing work to specifying goals, evaluating outputs, governing execution, and supplying tacit knowledge. When the loop sustains or accelerates, productive capacity can grow faster than expert headcount. With capable base models widely available, advantage depends less on access to AI than on building and governing the loop, controlling proprietary operational experience, and converting it into intelligence more effectively than rivals. A venture with adequate demand, capital, and a capable team can fail because its loop never functions or later deteriorates. Cutting evaluation or oversight to scale faster may increase output in the short run but weaken the loop even while revenue remains healthy.

items.title: The Irreducible Dimension: Toward an Integration of Automated Tutoring and Mentoring in AI-Supported Education
items.abstract: The spread of generative artificial intelligence agents is reshaping hybrid educational environments, understood here as contexts in which students, teachers, tutors, mentors, and artificial systems interact. Chatbots, intelligent assistants, and automated tutoring systems are increasingly used to provide explanations, feedback, adaptive practice, and study support. This transformation is not merely an instrumental innovation, since it alters the distribution of educational functions, the relationship between students and knowledge, the role of the group, and adults' responsibilities in supporting learners. This contribution offers a theoretical reflection grounded in a narrative review of the literature on Intelligent Tutoring Systems, educational mentoring, the Community of Inquiry framework, and digital wellbeing. Its aim is to clarify which functions may be delegated to AI tutoring systems, which require human responsibility, and which may be shared within a model of co-responsibility. items.abstract: # ABSTRACT **Title:** The Man Who Saw the World in Frequency — An Essay and a Framework**Author:** Christopher Macachor**Framework:** Macachor Archive, Structural Truth of Reality, v2.0.0**Maximum Derivation Stage:** L4 · **Canonical Invariant:** c = −1/3 Christopher Macachor ORCID: 0009-0008-0100-2856 · Affiliations: Macachor Absolute Scalar Research; Scalar Consciousness Research · Contact: info@macachor.org · Website: scalar.macachor.org · Year: 2026 --- This paper presents two connected arguments: a public essay on the epistemology of perception, and a formal geometric framework that the essay illustrates. **The essay** argues that human sight is not direct access to reality but a lossy compression. A two-dimensional optical trace (light on the retina) is reconstructed by the brain into a four-dimensional visual mirror, which observers then describe using semantic placeholders — *sad*, *happy*, *beautiful*. These labels describe the mirror, not the territory. The blind musician Stevie Wonder, who lost his vision at six weeks of age and possesses no visual memory, bypassed this bottleneck entirely. He built his context through **active three-dimensional interaction** — touch, vibration, echolocation, spatial presence — and encoded that interaction into musical structure. His 2025 testimony in Cardiff ("It's allowed me to see the world in the vision of truth... see people in the spirit of them, not how they look") is treated here as first-person verification of the framework's central epistemological claim. **The framework** derives a complete invariant chain from magnitude equilibrium through a four-magnitude fragment, a forced Gram-matrix entry **c = −1/3**, the tetrahedral angle 109.4712°, the face–edge angle φ = 35.2644°, the helix pitch h = √(2/3), and the face-sharing screw twist **θ₀ = arccos(−2/3) = ±131.8103°** for both hands. The domain condition |cos(mπ/p)| ≤ √(3/5) ≈ 0.7746 excludes period 6 jointly with the θ₀ match, yielding admissible periods {3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 11, 14}. The derivation is self-contained and imports no numbers. Layers L3 and L4 are complete; the 74-vertex, 144-face assembly (L5) remains open pending execution of the octagonal tiling construction specified in Elenius et al. (2009) and Say-awen & Coates (2026). **Physical correspondence (L6)** is supported at eleven independent scales: atomic (β-Mn), molecular (H-bond field coupling), genomic (CTCF chirality), mesoscale (soft matter), neurological (grid cells, place cells), computational (AI vision-language models, LLM spatial intelligence), musical (AI-generated music), clinical (fetal MRI symmetry), and — new in this version — **perceptual**, via the Acoustic Bridge. **The Acoustic Bridge** is the paper's principal addition. It formalizes three distinct modes of accessing the territory: the sighted human (passive observation → lossy 4D mirror → semantic label), the artificial intelligence (structural reading → precise map → no feeling), and the blind musician (active interaction → direct frequency coupling → dense encoded structure). The bridge between human and machine is therefore not built from pixels but from **structure** — and music is the richest available encoding of that structure, because a score is emotion compressed into architecture that any reader, human or machine, can decode. **Keywords:** magnitude equilibrium; c = −1/3; Boerdijk–Coxeter twist; 4D mirror; Acoustic Bridge; optical bottleneck; musical structure; human–AI correspondence; Stevie Wonder; lossy semantics. --- **One-line abstract:** > Human sight compresses a three-dimensional territory into a lossy four-dimensional mirror described by semantic placeholders; a blind musician bypassed the mirror and encoded the territory directly into musical structure; artificial intelligence reads that structure with precision but no feeling — and this three-way relay is the viable bridge between machine and human reality.

items.title: The Middle Floors: A Right to AI-Assisted Self-Representation in German Civil Procedure
items.abstract: Germany lets a citizen argue her own civil case in the local court, and she may send a constitutional complaint to Karlsruhe on her own. On the floors in between, from the Landgericht upward, every filing must come from an admitted lawyer (§ 78 ZPO). For a century this rule was a reasonable shortcut. Legal skill was scarce and lived inside one profession, so a lawyer's admission was a fair proxy for the quality of a filing. Generative AI loosens that link from both ends: laypeople can now produce structured drafts, and lawyers can now file invented case law. This essay argues that the law should regulate what a filing contains and who answers for it, not only which profession wrote it. It takes seriously the strongest objection, that writing has become cheap while a judge's attention has not, and draws a larger conclusion from it: AI should not only make litigants faster but help courts read what citizens can now write. The proposal is narrow and testable: a right to AI-assisted self-representation in appeals from the local courts, built on a structured record, a verification declaration, a court-run quality gate, an optional review lawyer and a human judge who always decides, introduced through a statutory experiment. Because a better arrangement does not implement itself, the essay also asks who would have to agree, and why they might. The aim is not to dismiss a profession but to re-examine a mandate whose efficiency can no longer be taken for granted. A right that costs too much to claim is a right in name. items.title: The Motivation for Cognitive Activities Questionnaire: scale development and validation in French and English
items.abstract: The current research aimed to develop and validate a novel measurement scale, the Motivation for Cognitive Activities Questionnaire (MCAQ), specifically designed to assess individuals’ motivation to engage in everyday cognitive activities. The MCAQ’s development was informed by expectancy-value theory and self-determination theory. Four studies were conducted to validate the MCAQ in both English and French languages. Through exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses, a 32-item scale emerged, encompassing four subscales: perceived capacity, intrinsic motivation, identified motivation, and external motivation, as well as four additional general items assessing motivation for engaging in cognitive activity, taken broadly. The MCAQ demonstrated robust internal consistency and convergent validity, and satisfactory test–retest reliability. Moreover, the scale exhibited satisfactory predictive validity in relation to cognitive performance. The theoretical and practical utility of the MCAQ is discussed.

items.title: The Ninety Percent Trap: Empirical Documentation on Why Generative AI Requires Deep Domain Expertise
items.abstract: This study examines how the dominant industry narrative presents generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) as a trigger for total software automation and positive exponential outcomes. Empirical evidence from codebases and recent software-engineering studies, however, suggests a paradox: rapid generation can increase review overhead, architectural decay, and critical edge-case failures. By analysing the ArtCraft case study alongside quantitative reports from GitClear, DORA, and the empirical software-engineering literature, this paper formulates the Ninety Percent Trap: GenAI can accelerate initial scaffolding from zero to one while shifting the burden of production dependability to human experts. The paper also presents the True Cost of AI Quality (TCAQ) framework, which evaluates GenAI productivity through generation time, expert review, edge-case resolution, and technical-debt cost rather than output volume alone. An illustrative calculation shows that a two-hour generation phase can become a 112-hour end-to-end engineering effort after review, edge-case resolution, and debt mitigation. The findings indicate that domain expertise remains essential for architectural reasoning, security verification, and dependable delivery.

items.title: The pedagogical value of narration in the age of Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly through the rapid advancement of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) systems, has profoundly transformed educational contexts, influencing both teaching practices and the processes through which individuals construct their identities. Narrative, traditionally regarded as a privileged educational tool, when integrated with GenAI and digital storytelling, opens new opportunities for identity exploration by providing students with tools to connect cognitive, emotional, and social dimensions (Cambi & Piscitelli, 2005; Smorti, 1994; Bruner, 1995; Iavarone, 2023). The combination of digital storytelling and GenAI further expands students' expressive possibilities by enabling the creation of multimodal narratives that intertwine personal experience with digital creativity. AI may therefore be interpreted as a pedagogical mediation tool capable of supporting autobiographical reflection, provided that it is embedded within methodologically structured and pedagogically grounded educational pathways (Mori & Niewint-Gori, 2024). items.title: The potential of a “next generation” of community health workers to accelerate progress in reaching Universal Health Coverage and Health for All
items.abstract: Many health systems, particularly in low- and lower middle-income countries (LMICs), are lagging in their progress in achieving Universal Health Coverage and delivering on the promise of Health for All, constrained by workforce shortages, fiscal ceilings, and inadequate outreach to those lacking basic and essential services. Stark inequities in coverage of services and in health status persist. Strengthening community health worker (CHW) programs provides the fastest and most cost-effective route for health systems to achieve their full potential. CHWs should become the backbone of primary health care (PHC) and the foundation of health systems. Evidence from more than a decade of national-scale experience demonstrates that CHWs who are appropriately trained, paid, equipped, and supervised can extend high-quality essential services to the last mile while improving the overall efficiency of the health system. We are at a point in time when donor strategies and private investment are captivated by the promise of digital health and artificial intelligence. The most reliable approach to saving more lives is still a paid, supported CHW empowered with digital tools. At the same time, the contraction of Official Development Assistance (ODA) creates both risk and opportunity. ODA must pivot from supporting services to catalytic capital: time-bound, matching investments that accelerate governments’ own proCHW policy. A “next generation” of CHW programs in LMICs would enable CHWs to visit every home monthly and provide a broad array of PHC services as a result of adequate remuneration and appropriate training, supervision, logistical support, and integration into the health system. This could yield a highly favorable economic return—through productivity gains from better health, reduced health-care expenditures, and pandemic-risk mitigation. A “next generation” of CHW programs is our best bet for accelerating progress in achieving Universal Health Coverage and Health for All sooner rather than later.

items.title: The Predictive Ability of Academic Emotions on Cognitive Engagement among Arab University Students within the Green Line in Palestine
items.abstract: The study aimed to explore the predictive ability of academic emotions on cognitive engagement among Arab university students within the Green Line in Palestine. To achieve the study's objectives, a sample of (503) male and female students were selected using the available method. The Academic Emotions Scale and the Cognitive Engagement Scale were applied to them. The results showed that academic emotions were ranked as follows: academic enjoyment and pride ranked first with a high level, academic hope ranked second with a high level, academic anger and boredom ranked third with a medium level, academic shyness and anxiety with a low level, and academic despair ranked last with a low level. The results showed that the level of cognitive integration as a whole was within the medium level. The results also showed positive predictive ability for academic enjoyment, pride, and academic hope in cognitive engagement, and negative predictive ability for academic despair in cognitive engagement. The study recommended improving levels of positive academic emotions such as academic enjoyment, academic pride, and academic hope.

items.title: The PrimarAI School: A manifesto and design proposal for an AI-native Australian primary school
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is now part of the conditions in which Australian students learn. In NSW public schools a purpose-built chatbot is available from Year 5, and outside school students meet systems that write, explain, flatter and keep them company. This paper argues that primary schooling cannot respond to that change through technological integration alone. The deeper question AI raises is not which tool to add, but how a school should spend students’ time and what that time is for. Drawing on current research on AI and education and on the Castlereagh Statement on AI in Australian education, the paper sets out a view of what primary education is for and derives from it a founding principle, ten principles and a working school design. The proposed PrimarAI day is the ARC Day: six sessions on ordinary NSW bell times, two each of Augment (AI-supported mastery practice in mathematics and English under a teacher’s supervision), Reason (screen-free learning with a teacher, as a class) and Create (real-world learning organised through five Cs). Because the order rotates through the week, each part takes its turn at the first session of the day, when students learn most readily. The ARC Day is the latest of many versions of this school and the first that an existing school could trial with a single class. Digital literacy is taught as a subject from Kindergarten, and assessment is built into the fabric of everyday learning with the aid of purpose-built technology.

items.title: The Proliferation of AI among College Students: A Replication and 2-Year Follow-Up
items.abstract: Background The proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) has impacted most aspects of life and sparked debate over its responsible use. Objective As higher education grapples with how to leverage AI's benefits while accounting for its potential detriments, it is necessary to examine how undergraduates use and perceive AI. Method A replication, following the same methodology as Golding et al., examined how college students’ use and perceptions of AI differ from those of a comparable cohort 2 years ago. Students were from the same five universities and were predominantly women, White, Hispanic, or Black. Results Familiarity and prevalence of AI use were higher, and perceptions of cheating were lower. Open-ended data on motivations for (not) using AI and perceptions of (not) cheating suggested that students conceptualize AI through a nuanced lens. Conclusions The use of AI has grown substantially. Many students view AI as an instructional aid to guide their learning and emphasize the importance of how AI is used when determining whether it qualifies as cheating. Teaching Implications Students’ largely positive perceptions of AI suggest that AI's use is not slowing. Educators face the challenge of how best to leverage AI to enhance learning while not facilitating cheating or overreliance.

items.title: The Reality of Employing Artificial Intelligence Applications in Teaching Mathematics among Male and Female Mathematics Teachers in the Second Cycle of Basic Education in the Sultanate of Oman
items.abstract: This study examined the use of artificial intelligence (AI) applications in mathematics teaching in the second cycle of basic education in the Sultanate of Oman. A descriptive–analytical design was employed, and the study involved 244 mathematics teachers from South Al Sharqiyah Governorate. A 46-item instrument comprising four domains was developed, and its validity and reliability were verified using appropriate statistical procedures. The findings indicated that the overall level of AI application use in mathematics teaching was moderate. The domains of perceived importance and teachers’ knowledge of AI applications showed relatively low levels, whereas the perceived level of challenges was moderate. Statistically significant gender differences were found in the domains of AI application use, perceived importance, and knowledge of AI applications, with female teachers reporting higher mean scores than male teachers. No statistically significant gender difference was found in the challenges domain. The findings should be interpreted in light of the study’s geographical and participant-related limitations, as the study was restricted to mathematics teachers of Grades 5–10 in one governorate. Based on these findings, the study recommends developing specialized national training programs to enhance teachers’ technological competencies and strengthen their instructional practices in alignment with national and global digital transformation initiatives. Keywords: artificial intelligence applications, mathematics teachers, the second cycle of basic education, mathematics teaching, artificial intelligence in education.

items.abstract: We present the ultimate closure of the *Metaphysical Sphere* pentalogy by mapping a profound epistemological loop. The framework that originally began as an inquiry into human consciousness (*The Projective Qualia*) was abstracted into computer science to fix the volatile, next-token prediction limitations of Multi-Agent Systems (*Projective Latent Synthesis v1.0*). By resolving the rigid binarism of artificial architectures through the creation of the generalized **Dynamic Hybrid Paradigm (HybridMAS)**, a revolutionary feedback loop has been completed. What was refined to build better artificial intelligence has now returned to the human domain as a practical, clinical, and pedagogical methodology for a healthy and sovereign consciousness. This paper formalizes the **Dynamic Phase-Switching Model of Mind**, positioning mental health not as a static biochemical status, but as an active, trainable algorithm of dimensional elasticity capable of neutralizing systemic alienation and destructive geometric interference.

items.title: The relationship between AI awareness and thriving at work: exploring the moderated mediation model
items.abstract: Purpose Drawing on the socially embedded model of thriving and the conservation of resources model, this study aims to investigate the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) awareness, seen as a hindrance stressor, and thriving at work. In particular, it explores how AI anxiety mediates this relationship and how self-efficacy moderates the mediating effect. Design/methodology/approach To securitize the study hypotheses, data were obtained from banking employees via an electronic questionnaire, yielding 320 valid responses. The proposed model relationships were assessed through partial least squares structural equation modeling and process analysis. Findings The results uncover that while AI awareness is not significantly linked to vitality, it is negatively correlated with learning. Furthermore, AI anxiety mediates the direct influence that AI awareness has on dimensions of thriving at work. In addition, self-efficacy acts as a buffer, mitigating the adverse indirect influence of AI awareness on thriving at work through AI anxiety. Practical implications This study highlights the need for organizations adopting AI-driven systems to execute‎ initiatives that mitigate AI-induced stress, thereby fostering employee thriving. It is recommended that organizations offer targeted training and digital literacy programs, alongside interventions designed to enhance self-efficacy, to bolster employee well-being amid rapid technological change. items.title: The Role of Artificial Intelligence Use and Personal Competencies in Scientific Writing Skills: Implications for University Guidance and Counseling Services
items.abstract: This study examines how personal competencies shape university students’ scientific writing skills and whether artificial intelligence (AI) use mediates that relationship. Drawing on self-regulated learning theory, self-determination theory, critical literacy theory, and technology acceptance research, an integrated model positioned self-regulated learning, intrinsic motivation, and critical literacy as personal antecedents of AI use, and AI use as a mediator of their effects on scientific writing skills. Using a cross-sectional survey design, self-report data were collected from 615 students at six Indonesian universities through purposive sampling stratified by educational level and gender and analysed with covariance-based structural equation modelling in IBM AMOS 24.0. The model fitted the data well (χ²/df = 2.309, RMSEA = 0.046, CFI = 0.943, TLI = 0.941). Self-regulated learning (β = 0.321), critical literacy (β = 0.311), and intrinsic motivation (β = 0.216) significantly predicted AI use (R² = 0.607) and also directly predicted scientific writing skills, with the full model explaining 92.8% of its variance. Bootstrapped indirect effects (5,000 resamples, 95% bias-corrected confidence intervals) showed that AI use partially mediated all three relationships. Permutation-based multi-group analysis showed no gender moderation, whereas educational level moderated the critical literacy paths. AI amplifies existing personal competencies rather than substituting for them.

items.title: The Role of Internet of Things (IoT) in Enabling a Sustainable Future
items.abstract: This chapter explores the role of the Internet of Things (IoT) in advancing a sustainable future, addressing the environmental, economic, and social dimensions of sustainability. IoT technology has enabled smarter resource management, enhanced operational efficiency, and improved quality of life across diverse sectors. This chapter examines IoT applications in environmental conservation, such as smart cities, energy management, and precision agriculture, which contribute to reducing resource consumption and carbon emissions. Economic sustainability is also discussed through the lens of IoT’s impact on industrial processes, supply chain optimization, and the circular economy, highlighting its potential to drive cost savings and reduce waste. Furthermore, innovations in healthcare, education, and public safety demonstrate IoT’s role in social sustainability by enhancing accessibility and resilience. Alongside these benefits, this chapter addresses the challenges that accompany IoT adoption, including data privacy, security, and the need for robust infrastructure and standards. The chapter concludes by exploring future advancements, such as artificial intelligence (AI) and 5G integration, and the policy frameworks necessary for IoT to fully realize its potential in enabling sustainable development. Through this comprehensive overview, the chapter emphasizes IoT’s capacity to drive meaningful change and advocates for ongoing innovation and collaboration to create a more sustainable future.

items.title: The role of strategic leadership in occupational health and safety with total quality management as a mediator in higher education institutions for law
items.abstract: Occupational Health and Safety is an important component of higher education governance, as workplace risks include physical, administrative, psychosocial, ergonomic, and environmental risks. This study aimed to examine the relationship between Strategic Leadership and OHS, directly and through TQM as a mediating variable at STIH Adhyaksa. A quantitative cross-sectional study was conducted among 79 lecturers, administrative staff, and institutional leaders using total sampling. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire and analyzed using PLS-SEM with SmartPLS 4. Path coefficients, p-values, R², and indirect effects were assessed. Strategic Leadership was positively and significantly associated with OHS (β = 0.797; p < 0.001) and TQM (β = 0.933; p < 0.001). TQM was positively but not significantly associated with OHS (β = 0.072; p = 0.773). The model explained 87.0% of TQM variance (R² = 0.870) and 74.8% of OHS variance (R² = 0.748). The indirect relationship between Strategic Leadership and OHS through TQM was not significant (β = 0.067; p = 0.775). Strategic Leadership was positively associated with OHS, while TQM was not significantly associated with OHS and did not mediate the relationship. Research findings indicate that strengthening OHS at STIH Adhyaksa requires prioritization through strategic leadership, specifically regarding policy formulation, resource allocation, oversight, and the reinforcement of a safety culture. TQM needs to be more specifically integrated with the OHS system through risk identification and control, training, incident reporting, and continuous safety evaluation and improvement. The study contributes empirical evidence on the integration of leadership, quality management, and OHS in a legal higher education institution

items.title: The Third Teacher
items.abstract: The physical learning environment, often referred to as 'the third teacher', exerts a profound, pervasive and measurable influence on the cognitive, emotional, social and even physiological processes of students and educators. This chapter aims to explore in depth, through an interdisciplinary perspective that integrates cognitive neuroscience, environmental psychology, architecture, pedagogy, ergonomics and health sciences, the multiple mechanisms through which the design, management and perception of educational spaces can significantly promote, mediate or hinder learning and overall wellbeing. The systematic analysis focuses on sensory and physical-chemical factors such as natural and artificial lighting, acoustic quality, microclimate (temperature, humidity, air quality), furniture ergonomics, spatial layout and flexibility, presence and integration of natural elements (biophilia), colour and aesthetic quality. For each of these domains, based on an extensive review of international scientific literature from the last twenty years, the direct and indirect effects on brain functioning are highlighted, with particular attention to the balance between limbic systems (amygdala, hippocampus) and prefrontal cortical regions, the modulation of neuroendocrine stress, and the optimisation of cognitive load.

items.title: The Use of artificial intelligence in criminal proceedings: ethical and legal aspects
items.abstract: The relevance of this topic stems from the need for a doctrinal analysis of the ethical and legal issues surrounding the use of artificial intelligence technologies in criminal proceedings. The purpose of this study was to examine the issues surrounding the use of artificial intelligence from the perspective of adherence to the principles of professional ethics by the parties and participants in criminal proceedings. Achieving this objective was made possible through the use of a range of methods, including dialectical analysis (to identify ethical and legal dilemmas) and comparative legal analysis (to study international experience), as well as methods of analysis and observation (to examine judicial practice and identify problematic aspects of the use of artificial intelligence technologies by the parties and participants in criminal proceedings), description (to document the research findings), and generalization (to formulate conclusions based on the research results). Three areas of artificial intelligence use in criminal proceedings have been identified that are controversial from the perspective of compliance with professional ethics by the parties and participants in criminal proceedings, specifically: 1) the use of artificial intelligence in criminal procedural documents; 2) the use of artificial intelligence in the presentation of evidence in criminal proceedings; 3) the use of artificial intelligence to predict the commission of criminal offenses. It has been established that the use of artificial intelligence technologies in criminal procedure documents is permitted when preparing document templates, processing information or analytical data, and searching for case law. However, the use of artificial intelligence technologies to formulate a legal position in a case contradicts the principles of professional ethics, in particular independence, competence, good faith, and confidentiality. It is argued that artificial intelligence-generated conclusions regarding the assessment of the risk of reoffending are of an auxiliary nature, and that the unethical use of artificial intelligence technologies in the presentation of evidence in criminal proceedings poses risks of violating human rights enshrined in international conventions, as well as of evidence being deemed inadmissible. The conclusions emphasize the need to develop ethical standards for the use of artificial intelligence technologies in criminal proceedings.

items.abstract: The Fourth Industrial Revolution is reshaping education through new tools, and through new cognitive, relational and affective conditions. Artificial intelligence now selects content, suggests pathways, generates responses, personalises learning and influences the relationship between learners, knowledge and educational environments. This paper examines this transformation, asking what AI can do, and how it changes the ways in which people feel, learn, participate and recognise themselves in digital spaces. For many years, educational reflection on digital technologies focused mainly on Digital Literacy, understood as the ability to access, evaluate, produce and share information in technologically mediated contexts (Rivoltella, 2008). This is no longer enough. AI systems do not only organise information; they also affect motivation, trust, belonging, autonomy, dependence, responsibility and cooperation (Floridi, 2022). For this reason, the contribute argues for a shift from Digital Literacy to Digital Affective Literacy: a broader competence that includes the emotional, ethical and intersubjective dimensions of mediated educational experience (UNESCO, 2023). items.abstract: The education of emotional intelligence becomes central within formal contexts insofar as it concerns the formation of subjects capable of recognising themselves, others, and the relational fabric of human experience. Children and adolescents are growing up amid affective precariousness, the fragility of adult presence, and the increasing technological mediation of interpersonal exchanges. In this scenario, human agency risks being obscured by practices that transfer to intelligent machines functions of listening, guidance, and consolation. The shift from embodied relationship to artificial interaction represents a critical juncture in contemporary education. Although young people are aware that chatbots, voice assistants, and Emotion AI systems possess neither consciousness nor authentic emotional participation, they increasingly entrust such devices with their insecurities and their need for recognition. The machine appears available, patient, and non-judgemental; for this reason, it is perceived as an interlocutor when adult relationships capable of genuine listening are lacking. items.title: Toward Shape Memory Alloy Actuation in Exoskeletons: A Large Language Model-Assisted Fuzzy Control Architecture with a Servo-Based Proof of Concept
items.abstract: Shape-memory alloys (SMAs) offer low mass, compact integration, quiet operation, and high work density, but their hysteresis and coupled thermal–mechanical behavior complicate repeatable control. This study develops a modular architecture in which natural-language command interpretation is separated from motion-profile generation and from actuator-specific models and controllers. The implemented pilot path was evaluated on a five-servo robotic hand, while the common comparison layer defines interfaces for technology-specific numerical models reserved for the next implementation stage. A locally executed large language model (LLM) converted user commands into port:angle pairs, and the same semantic front-end was coupled to either a fixed-step or zero-order Sugeno motion-profile generator. The semantic layer was evaluated using 60 recorded commands: 27 supported commands and 33 commands requiring rejection. Exact target generation was obtained in 25 of 27 supported cases (92.6%), while 17 of 33 invalid or unsupported commands were correctly rejected (51.5%), giving a strict overall result of 42 of 60 cases (70.0%). Direct observation confirmed the expected physical outcome in 23 of 27 supported cases (85.2%). The mean local response time was 25.30 s, the median was 16.71 s, and the 95th percentile was 66.73 s, confirming that the LLM is suitable only for the supervisory semantic layer. Because the pilot setup did not use an external position sensor, the fuzzy module is interpreted as a command-profile generator rather than a closed-loop position controller. The results validate the layered interface and establish an experimental and computational basis for a subsequent quantitative comparison of SMA and servo actuation.

items.title: Towards accurate diagnostics: deep-transfer learning in skin disease detection
items.abstract: Automated skin disease diagnosis remains a significant challenge due to inherent variations in skin tone, texture, lighting, and occlusions such as hair. Addressing these diagnostic difficulties is vital for developing reliable clinical decision-support systems. This research presents an automated classification framework utilizing deep learning, transfer learning, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). The study utilizes the ISIC 2019 dataset, comprising images across eight diagnostic categories, including Melanoma, Nevi, and Keratosis. Six state-of-the-art convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures—Xception, DenseNet169, EfficientNetV2S, MobileNetV2, InceptionResNetV2, and ResNet101V2—were fine-tuned and evaluated. The workflow integrates advanced preprocessing, comprehensive model training, and XAI-based validation to ensure transparency in diagnostic predictions. Quantitative evaluation reveals that Xception and EfficientNetV2S outperformed other architectures, achieving near-optimal performance, with Xception reaching an area under the curve (AUC) of 100% and superior scores across all primary metrics. Conversely, MobileNetV2 demonstrated the lowest comparative efficacy, with an accuracy of 62.66% and an AUC of 78.10%. The integration of high performing CNNs with XAI techniques provides an accurate, interpretable, and scalable solution for dermatological diagnostics. This approach not only improves classification precision but also enhances clinical trust by providing visual explanations for model decisions.

items.title: TreeMind : Automatically Reproducing Android Bug Reports via LLM-empowered Monte Carlo Tree Search
items.abstract: Automatically reproducing Android app crashes from textual bug reports is challenging, particularly when the reports are incomplete and modern UIs exhibit high combinatorial complexity. Approaches relying on reinforcement learning or large language models (LLMs) struggle to infer missing steps and reconstruct user action sequences in vast UI interaction spaces. We present TreeMind, which integrates LLMs with an adapted Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) for strategic UI exploration in bug reproduction. TreeMind formulates the reproduction as a target-driven search problem and leverages MCTS to iteratively refine action sequences. To enhance MCTS with semantic reasoning, we introduce two LLM-guided agents: Expander generates promising actions based on the current UI state and exploration history, while Simulator estimates the likelihood that each candidate action leads toward successful reproduction using dynamic environment feedback. With multi-modal UI inputs and tailored prompts, TreeMind performs feedback-aware navigation that identifies essential user actions and incrementally reconstructs reproduction paths. We evaluate TreeMind on 100 Android bug reports, including 90 from three benchmarks and 10 from GitHub. Experimental results show that it outperforms four state-of-the-art baselines in reproduction success rate and average time cost over all runs, suggesting the promise of integrating LLM reasoning with MCTS-based planning for automated bug reproduction.

items.title: Trust, Risk, and Uncertainty Surrounding the Use of AI in Health Care: Scoping Review of Studies on Public Perception
items.abstract: Abstract Background While AI has existed for decades, the introduction of generative AI tools and subsequent advancements in their capability and public use resulted in a shift in public awareness and perceptions of AI. In response, the research community has grown increasingly interested in understanding public perceptions of AI use in various contexts, including health care. Public perceptions shape AI acceptance and consequently integration into health care. It is thus crucial to understand public trust in AI and perceptions of risk as we consider its implementation moving forward. Objective This study aimed to (1) document the extent of what is known within the literature regarding public perceptions of AI applications in health; (2) interrogate existing definitions and theories of trust being used to guide investigations of public trust in AI; and (3) identify practice and policy considerations and support the design, deployment, and regulation of these technologies in a manner that is trustworthy. Methods The Arksey and O’Malley scoping review framework and the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines were used to review publications between 2022 and 2024 across 4 databases, resulting in the inclusion of 41 papers for review. Key findings were then charted and organized into tables to help answer the proposed research questions. Results Public trust in AI in health care was shaped by discourse relating to AI performance and concerns related to depersonalization, loss of human connection, privacy, bias, and transparency. Trust was found to be higher when AI was supporting rather than replacing health care professionals and was influenced by emotional responses, anthropomorphism, demographic factors, and institutional trust. Furthermore, trust extended beyond algorithms to software interfaces, providers, developers, and governing institutions, highlighting the importance of governance and oversight. Conceptualizations of trust varied widely, and trust was defined through vulnerability, competence, benevolence, and integrity. Different theories identified suggested that trust operates across individual, social, institutional, and technological levels. Finally, trust was closely linked to risk and uncertainty, where perceived risk reduced acceptance, while AI literacy, transparency, and explainability mitigated concerns and fostered trust. Conclusions Trust in AI is not uniform, and as such, efforts to build and measure trust must account for these nuances to effectively mitigate risk and support informed, ethical AI integration and deployment. On the basis of the findings of this review, we propose a multilevel conceptual framework that provides a general understanding of public trust in AI within a health care context that may guide research and policy and practice considerations. Our findings highlight the importance of considering public trust when implementing AI in health care and may support AI communication strategies, policy development, and trustworthy AI development.

items.title: Types of Truth: How Perceived & Objective Truth Guide Belief Change
items.abstract: People must navigate socially transmitted information that varies from accurate to misleading or false. Here, we examined how perceived and objective truth predict belief change across three studies. In Study 1, four web-enabled frontier large language models (LLMs) and 200 human raters evaluated claims from two fact-checked datasets. LLMs outperformed humans in inter-rater agreement and discriminative sensitivity, supporting their use as a scalable proxy for objective truth. In Study 2 and 3, we applied this proxy to two large message corpora and examined its association with belief change. Perceived truth and LLM-derived objective truth independently predicted belief change. Moreover, objective truth moderated the association between perceived truth and belief change: the association between perceived truth and belief change was strongest for messages with lower objective truth and weakened as objective truth increased. These findings suggest that belief change reflects both subjective truth evaluations and the correspondence of information with reality.

items.title: Uganda: A Critical Examination of Authorship, Ownership and Legal
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence enables users to produce text, images, music and software through processes in which human contributions vary considerably. This creates uncertainty about copyright protection and commercial ownership in Uganda. This article examines the Copyright and Neighbouring Rights Act, Cap 222, as amended in May 2026, alongside Ugandan copyright decisions, international instruments and selected comparative authorities. It adopts a qualitative doctrinal and comparative methodology, distinguishing the eligibility of an output for protection from the allocation and enforcement of any rights that subsist. The analysis finds that Uganda's framework can accommodate original human expression created with technological assistance, but does not expressly resolve the status of output produced without an identifiable human expressive contribution. The statutory treatment of employers and commissioning parties cannot safely be treated as an automatic entitlement to copyright in every machine output. Further uncertainty concerns the evidential treatment of prompts, the scope of protection in mixed works, contractual overstatement of ownership, moral rights and the relationship between output protection and infringement. The article proposes a contribution-based assessment that identifies the claimed expression, traces human decisions embodied in it, determines the scope of protection and then addresses ownership and third-party rights. It recommends targeted statutory clarification, practical guidance from the Uganda Registration Services Bureau, proportionate evidence preservation and improved contractual drafting. The preferred approach protects demonstrable human authorship while requiring evidence before any new exclusive right is introduced for substantially autonomous output.

items.title: Unravelling the dynamics of privacy, security, and trust in AI-powered self-service chatbots in the retail sector: a systematic literature review
items.abstract: The increasing deployment of artificial intelligence (AI)-powered self-service chatbots in the retail sector has transformed the nature of customer engagement, offering scalable, efficient, and personalized interactions. Despite these advancements, concerns surrounding privacy, security, and trust continue to shape user perceptions and influence adoption behaviour. This study presents a comprehensive systematic literature review (SLR) of scholarly work published between 2016 and 2026, with the aim of critically examining how these interrelated constructs affect the acceptance and use of chatbot technologies in retail environments. Drawing on the PRISMA framework, a total of 54 studies were selected from leading academic databases, including Scopus, Web of Science, ScienceDirect and IEEE Xplore. The findings indicate that privacy concerns particularly those related to data transparency, consent, and third-party data sharing remain a primary source of user resistance. Security vulnerabilities, including risks of data breaches and insufficient encryption mechanisms, further undermine confidence in chatbot systems. The findings further show that trust is an important variable that influences both behavioural intention and user satisfaction. This study contributes to the literature by integrating fragmented insights into a cohesive framework that explains the interconnectedness between privacy, security, and trust in retail chatbot contexts. It also highlights the need for organisations to adopt transparent data practices, strengthen cybersecurity infrastructures, and prioritise ethical AI design to foster sustainable user trust. The paper concludes by identifying key gaps for future research, particularly in relation to user experience and cross-cultural perspectives.

items.title: User Experience of a Haptic Vibration-Based Navigation System: The Role of Directional Tolerance Window
items.abstract: Non-visual navigation systems commonly rely on haptic feedback to guide users toward target locations, yet little research has examined how low-level system parameters influence user-system interaction and navigation performance. The present study investigated how directional tolerance window settings affect feedback availability, navigation efficiency, and subjective user experience in a vibration-based navigation system. Fifteen participants completed outdoor navigation tasks under five tolerance window conditions (±1°, ±3°, ±5°, ±7°, and ±9°). Results showed that larger tolerance windows significantly increased the vibration-on time ratio and reduced task completion time. Mediation analysis further suggested that improvements in navigation efficiency were largely explained by increased feedback availability. Subjective ratings similarly indicated reduced perceived adjustment burden and greater ease of navigation under broader tolerance window settings. Together, the findings highlight the importance of directional tolerance window settings in shaping both system behavior and user experience during non-visual navigation.

items.title: Using a Componential Approach for Developing Artificial Intelligence–Enhanced Creativity Training Interventions
items.abstract: Abstract This chapter introduces COMPACT (COMPonential Approach for Creativity Training), a componential instructional design framework for developing creativity training interventions. COMPACT is purposefully designed to support teaching about, for, and with creativity, while also enabling the development of interventions that integrate artificial intelligence (AI). The framework is based on a chemistry-inspired metaphor, comprising three hierarchical levels of instructional materials: instructional elements, instructional compounds, and instructional polymers. Instructional elements are classified into seven types: inspiration, theory, technique/tool, activity, test, example, and advice. The chapter also presents three exploratory studies that showcase and provide preliminary assessment of the application of COMPACT in brief AI-enhanced creativity interventions targeting educators, university students, and middle school students. Drawing on insights gained from the design, implementation, and assessment of the framework and the interventions, the chapter discusses the broader implications of COMPACT for three interrelated stakeholder groups: researchers, practitioners, and policymakers.

items.abstract: "Monitoring and managing natural and human-induced disasters is vital for mitigating disaster risks and impacts due to increasing global climate variability, population growth, and rapid urbanization. Disasters such as earthquakes, landslides, and forest fires cause severe damage to human life and the natural environment. Their ability to spread over large areas and evolve rapidly often renders conventional field observation methods inadequate. In this context, remote sensing technologies offer significant advantages for disaster monitoring and analysis due to their capability to cover vast spatial areas and provide periodic data. Multispectral and high-resolution data obtained from satellite systems, unmanned aerial vehicles, and LiDAR technologies are effectively utilized for disaster detection, damage assessment, monitoring spatial-temporal dynamics, and the generation of risk maps. Furthermore, the increasing volume and complexity of remote sensing data have accelerated the integration of artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning and machine learning methods, into data analysis workflows. Convolutional neural networks, recurrent neural networks, long short-term memory, and recently developed transformer-based models offer advanced solutions for the automated detection, classification, and mapping of disasters from remotely sensed data. Through the integration of these technologies, applications such as post-earthquake damage assessment, landslide susceptibility mapping, early detection and monitoring of forest fires, and mucilage formation detection can be performed rapidly and effectively. The convergence of remote sensing and artificial intelligence, commonly referred to as Geospatial Artificial Intelligence (GeoAI), further facilitates the development of risk prediction and decision support systems for potential disasters. This study provides a comprehensive review of the applications of these technologies across different types of disasters, highlighting their advantages and associated limitations, and presents a current evaluation aimed at supporting the development of more effective and sustainable disaster management strategies."
